I know you asked about cars in general, but I'm going to throw this out anyway.

If you plan on working on your specific car more in depth I recommend getting a factory service manual (FSM).

It will show you step by step how to do things and list torque values and technical specs for your car. So there will be less guess work compared to following a video that says "tighten it up snug," etc. It will help you feel confident. I have owned one for every car/motorcycle I've owned. Sometimes you can find PDF versions in a forum for your specific vehicle. I usually just hit up eBay or Amazon as I like having a hardcopy. They're usually used but still perfectly usable, and you're just going to get it dirty anyways.

Many things you learn on your car will carryover to other cars. Disk brakes, bleeding hydraulics, plugs, wires, troubleshooting coilpacks, fuses, relays, etc. The rabbit hole goes pretty deep.

This is what I did. My parents had a beat to heck civic when I was 17 and they told me if I could get it running well they'd let me drive it since they weren't using it at all. So I bought a Chilton repair manual specific to my car and I started looking into each individual problem with the car. Most repairs you'd do on a specific car are more or less the same on other cars, it's more often a variance in the design of the parts than the overall design of the engine. After keeping that civic running for two years I can pretty confidently do most jobs on any other car. I've done head gaskets, full swaps, valve adjustments, and a ton of less ambitious projects.

A factory service manual is best, but can be expensive if your car is still newer.

A Chilton or a Haynes manual will get you into it for pretty cheap (maybe $5-$20 depending on new/used), and they can be found at many auto parts stores or eBay/Amazon.

For something like $30 you can buy a year's access for one model to Alldata; this is one of the large professional information services that professional mechanics use. Most of the repair information in there is reprinted from the factory service info, and there are other resources such as technical service bulletins. Although older vehicles did have paper service manuals, for the last several years all manufacturer technical information has only been available in internet based electronic format. There is simply too much information, and too many frequent updates and changes to make publishing it in paper form feasible.
